text.en: Raju saw that table salt and sugar both dissolved in water. A classroom diagram showed charged particles in salt water and neutral sugar molecules in sugar water.

A chemical bond is an attraction that holds atoms or ions together in a stable arrangement. Some bonded substances form molecules, while others form extended structures. The Kossel–Lewis model uses valence electrons to describe bonding. The octet rule fits many main-group examples. The first shell is full with two electrons, and other exceptions also occur.
In an ionic or electrovalent bond one atom gives electrons and another takes them, forming positive and negative ions held by electrostatic attraction. The number of electrons lost or gained is the electrovalency. In magnesium chloride, magnesium has 2, 8, 2 and loses two electrons while each chlorine with 2, 8, 7 gains one.
In a covalent bond atoms share electrons. Lewis dot structures show the outer electrons as dots. Bonding and structure help explain a substance’s properties. The kinds of particles and how freely they can move also matter. Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons.

Valence electrons occupy the outer occupied shell in our simple shell pictures. Their arrangement helps us follow electron transfer and sharing in many chemical bonds.
Neon has two electrons in its first shell and eight in its second. Helium has only a first shell, which is complete with two electrons. These are useful reference patterns.
A Lewis symbol shows valence electrons as dots around an element’s symbol. Draw one dot for sodium and seven for chlorine in the simple model.
Track sodium from a neutral atom to a positive ion. When it loses one electron, the number of protons stays fixed, so it has one more positive than negative charge.
A chlorine atom that gains one electron becomes a chloride ion. Its negative charge comes from having one more electron than its proton count.
Opposite ionic charges attract. In solid sodium chloride, many sodium and chloride ions form a repeating three-dimensional arrangement. The formula shows one sodium ion per chloride ion.
For magnesium chloride, the magnesium ion has charge positive two. One chloride has only one negative charge. Add a second chloride to balance it.
Draw a calcium ion with positive two charge and an oxide ion with negative two. One of each balances the charge. Use the simplest whole-number ratio in the formula.
Ions in solid salt are held in the lattice. When a suitable ionic solid melts, its ions can move more freely. Mobile ions can carry an electric current.

When salt dissolves in water, its separated ions can move through the solution. A sugar solution has dissolved neutral molecules. The two solutions differ in the charged particles available to carry current.
For a covalent example, two hydrogen atoms share a pair of electrons. The shared pair counts toward the full first shell for each atom in the Lewis model.
Next, draw two chlorine atoms. Each contributes one electron to the shared pair. Each chlorine keeps three pairs of outer electrons that are not in the bond.

board.text: Cl–Cl: one shared pair and three lone pairs on each Cl

text.en: A double bond has two shared pairs. In the simple Lewis model of oxygen gas, each oxygen contributes to two such pairs between the atoms.
A triple bond has three shared pairs. The Lewis picture of nitrogen gas uses three bonds and keeps one lone pair on each nitrogen.
Water uses two single oxygen–hydrogen bonds in its Lewis picture. The remaining four outer electrons on oxygen appear as two lone pairs.

board.text: H–O–H with two oxygen lone pairs

text.en: In methane, carbon shares one pair with each of four hydrogen atoms. Count four shared pairs. Each hydrogen shares one pair with carbon.
For a coordinate bond, one partner supplies both electrons of the shared pair when the bond forms. In the course diagram, an ammonia molecule donates a lone pair to a hydrogen ion.

board.text: NH₃ can donate a lone pair to H⁺

text.en: The product in that example is ammonium. After the ion forms, its four nitrogen to hydrogen bonds are equivalent. The coordinate label describes how the pair was supplied.
In an electron-transfer example, losing electrons is oxidation and gaining them is reduction. The two processes occur together when electrons move from one species to another.

board.text: Oxidation loses electrons · reduction gains electrons

text.en: Follow a sodium atom losing one electron and another species accepting it. The sodium is oxidised while the partner is reduced. Count the same electron as it leaves one and arrives at the other.

board.text: Track the electron from donor to acceptor

text.en: Some molecular substances have low melting points because separating their molecules takes less energy than pulling apart a strong lattice. The bonds within each molecule can remain intact during melting.

board.text: Between-molecule attractions differ from bonds in a molecule

text.en: When reading a formula or dot diagram, first identify whether it shows a molecule or a repeating ratio. Then count shared pairs, or use the ion charges to check the overall balance.

board.text: Count pairs in molecules · balance charges in ion ratios

points.en: The octet rule describes many main-group examples. Hydrogen follows a two-electron first shell.
Ionic bond: transfer; covalent bond: sharing.
Oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons.
Bonding, structure and particle motion help explain properties.
